name: distcc
baseline: local single-machine compilation (make with every compile run locally); also plain distcc for the pump-mode rows
workload: Wall-clock make time (configure excluded) for binutils-2.18, glibc-2.6, httpd-2.0.43, linux-2.6.25, samba-3.0.20 and hello-2.1.1, built entirely locally versus distributed to 38 compile servers (152 CPUs) with make -j40, in plain mode and in pump mode (also -j80); each case run 5 times and averaged.
claimed_speedup: Linux 2.6.25: 818.3s local, 203.2s plain distcc (about 4.0x, derived from page data), 134.9s pump mode (about 6.1x, derived from page data). Samba 3.0.20: 314.0s local, 101.8s plain (about 3.1x, derived), 31.4s pump (about 10x, derived). glibc 2.6: 946.4s local, 534.0s plain, 357.8s pump. binutils 2.18: 125.8s local, 35.4s plain, 28.7s pump. httpd 2.0.43: 139.8s local, 85.1s plain, 80.1s pump. Page text: pump mode is sometimes more than 3x faster than plain distcc (Samba), and up to 2.5x faster than non-pump on 4-processor clients for large Google projects. hello-2.1.1 gets slower: 0.7s local, 0.9s plain, 1.1s pump.
hardware: Client: 2.8GHz Intel Pentium 4, 2G RAM, Linux 2.6.18.5 (modified Ubuntu 6.06). Servers: 38 machines described as 4 CPU 2GHz AMD Dual Core Processor 270 with 2G RAM (152 CPUs in total).
stars_or_usage: 2.3k stars; README says it has compiled the Linux kernel, KDE, GNOME and Samba, and run with hundreds of servers
tradeoffs: Needs the distccd daemon and a compatible compiler on every volunteer machine and a fast network (a slow network can cancel the gain). Plain mode ships preprocessed source and still preprocesses on the client; pump mode needs identical system headers on client and servers, assumes sources and headers do not change during the build, and falls back to plain distcc when it hits an error (the page says the Linux kernel needed special handling). Small projects get slower (hello-2.1.1). README.pump says pump mode will probably show no major gain with fewer than about ten CPUs. GPL licence.
caveats: First-party Google/distcc page dated 2008 (copyright line) on 2008-era hardware; compiler version and flags are not stated, so not tier A even though the harness lives in the repo (bench/ directory, contents not read). The local baseline is one single-core 2.8GHz Pentium 4 against 152 server CPUs, which inflates the ratio; the page itself says a multi-processor client would show smaller gains. Only make time is counted, not configure. The page notes pump runs that silently fell back to plain mode while collecting results. The ratios above marked derived are computed from the page's wall-time column. README.md separately claims three machines are 2.6 times faster than one and README.pump says pump mode is up to 10X faster than plain distcc for the compile step (not the whole build); neither number is on the benchmark page. No comparison with ccache, icecream or a modern build system.

name: doctest
workload: bench.py-generated CMake projects built single-threaded: (1) 201 source files with the framework header included in every file, (2) 50k CHECK(a==b) asserts across 10 files, (3) a runtime loop of 10 million passing CHECK(i == i) asserts, with and without INFO(i) logging.
claimed_speedup: Header cost: doctest.h costs 11ms-23ms per source file against 380ms-470ms for catch.hpp (page: more than 36 times lighter on MSVC). 201 files with header everywhere, Linux GCC Release: 11.05s vs 99.48s (baselines 4.29s vs 4.50s); MSVC Release: 8.71s vs 87.17s. 50k CHECK(a==b) asserts, Linux GCC Release: 257.40s vs 608.94s; MSVC Release: 58.73s vs 448.68s (page: between 0 and 8 times faster than Catch); with DOCTEST_CONFIG_SUPER_FAST_ASSERTS 97.46s on Linux GCC Release. Runtime 10M asserts: MSVC Release 0.40s vs 0.76s, Linux GCC Release 0.29s vs 0.29s, Linux Clang Release 0.28s vs 0.32s; with INFO logging Linux GCC Release 0.52s vs 3.60s (page: around 20% faster for plain asserts, a few times faster with logging).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 2017 15.8.1, MinGW GCC 8.1.0, Linux GCC 6.3.0, Linux Clang 4.0.0. scripts/bench/bench.py configures CMake with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Debug or Release (CMake default flags), adds -std=c++11 on non-MSVC and -w on GCC/Clang; no explicit -O flags; builds single-threaded with cmake --build.
hardware: Intel i7 3770k, 16G RAM; Windows 7 on an SSD, and Ubuntu 17.04 in a VirtualBox VM on a HDD
tradeoffs: Smaller feature set than Catch2 (modelled on Catch; the FAQ lists the differences, not read). The biggest assert-compile wins need the non-decomposing CHECK_EQ(a,b) form and the DOCTEST_CONFIG_SUPER_FAST_ASSERTS define, so they are not like-for-like with Catch's CHECK(a==b). DOCTEST_CONFIG_DISABLE strips tests from the binary. Single header, C++11.
caveats: The project's own benchmark (Dec 2018): doctest 2.2.0 against Catch 2.3.0, both far behind current releases; Catch2 v3 became a compiled library with a different compile-time profile and was not measured. Flags come from the public script rather than the page text, and there are no explicit optimisation flags. Linux numbers come from a VirtualBox VM on a HDD; no repeat counts or variance are given. Runtime for plain asserts is near parity on GCC and Clang Release (0.29s vs 0.29s); the large runtime win is only with INFO logging. README says compile time is better 'by orders of magnitude', while the tables show roughly 9-10x on whole-build header cost and up to about 8x on assert macros. Google Test and Boost.Test are not benchmarked on the page. The tier A rating rests on the public script plus stated compilers and CPU; a verifier may still downgrade it for the missing explicit flags.

name: icecream (icecc)
workload: make builds of Linux 2.6.16 (defconfig, many small C files) and the src/ subdirectory of Qt 3.3.6 (medium and large C++ files) on a two-machine icecream cluster, over 54MBit WLAN and 100MBit LAN, versus make on one machine with no icecream; 5 runs, worst and best dropped, middle 3 averaged.
claimed_speedup: Linux 2.6.16: 315s local (make -j1) vs 230s with icecream over WLAN (make -j10) and 203s over 100MBit LAN (make -j10/100); the file says the maximum improvement is 27% (LAN: 36%) out of a theoretical 50%. Qt 3.3.6 src/: 368s local (make -j1) vs 269s over WLAN (make -j10) and 239s over LAN (make -j10/100). Later note in the file (test project not named): remote with -m 1 at 0.8.0 took 257s for make -j5, and 442s without compression. Overhead of the wrapper without a cluster is about 2%.
hardware: Two single-CPU machines of about the same speed (1.7GHz Pentium M); otherwise idle 54MBit WLAN, repeated on 100MBit cabled LAN
stars_or_usage: 1.8k stars; created by SUSE based on distcc (per README)
tradeoffs: Needs iceccd on every node and a central scheduler (iceccd/icecc-scheduler); jobs ship preprocessed source and compiler environments across the network. README says the scheduler gives it advantages over distcc (idle-cycle scheduling, changing compiler versions, cross-compiling) but gives no numbers for that. A lone machine gains nothing: README's own test took 1.6s locally against 1.9s via icecream for one job, and BENCH calls running icecream without parallel make 'a horrible mistake' (make -j1 took 418s vs 315s local). GPL licence.
caveats: First-party BENCH file with results only, not scripts: no compiler version or flags, no CPU beyond 1.7GHz Pentium M, circa 2006 (mentions a 2006-06-16 branch) on a two-node cluster, much older than current icecream. The cluster has only two nodes, so the 27-36% gains are bounded by a theoretical 50%. Several rows are for development patches ('no-latency', 'make-it-cool' branch) and not a release. No measured comparison against distcc anywhere in the repo; the distcc comparison in README is qualitative. Percentages are quoted from the file's own text.

name: CMake unity (jumbo) builds
baseline: ordinary one-translation-unit-per-source CMake build (same target without UNITY_BUILD)
workload: Release build of the SpeedCrunch calculator target with CMake -DCMAKE_UNITY_BUILD=ON (default batch size 8) against the same build without unity, with three Windows compilers.
claimed_speedup: SpeedCrunch Release: about 29% speed-up with MinGW GCC 8.1.0, about 54% with Visual C++ 2017, about 24% with Clang-cl 8.0.0 (from a search summary of the Qt blog post; snippet only).
compiler_and_flags: MinGW GCC 8.1.0, Visual C++ 2017, Clang-cl 8.0.0 (versions per search summary); Release mode; flags not shown; CMake option -DCMAKE_UNITY_BUILD=ON
hardware: Windows 10 machine with an AMD Ryzen CPU (model not shown in the summary)
stars_or_usage: 8.1k stars (GitHub mirror of the upstream CMake repository); UNITY_BUILD ships since CMake 3.16
tradeoffs: Implemented in Source/cmLocalGenerator.cxx (AddUnityBuild) with UNITY_BUILD, UNITY_BUILD_BATCH_SIZE, UNITY_BUILD_MODE and SKIP_UNITY_BUILD_INCLUSION. CMake's own docs say projects should not set UNITY_BUILD or CMAKE_UNITY_BUILD directly; per the book lead, merged sources can clash on file-scope names and macros, and larger translation units cut parallelism, raise memory use and make incremental rebuilds recompile whole batches. Qt Creator's own sources were not unity-compatible per the post, which is why SpeedCrunch was measured.
caveats: Snippet only: www.qt.io could not be opened (host unresolvable from this container), so the three percentages come from WebSearch result summaries of the 2019-08-01 Qt blog post and need re-checking on the page. First-party style, single machine and one project, 2019, measured on the pre-release feature. The percentage definition (time saved or speed ratio) is not clear from the summary. The book's quoted 20-50% for Qt Creator could not be matched to that post: the summaries tie the unity figures to SpeedCrunch. The kitware/cmake repo carries the implementation and docs but no benchmark code or timings (Help/prop_tgt/UNITY_BUILD.rst has no numbers).

name: CMake precompiled headers (target_precompile_headers)
baseline: ordinary one-translation-unit-per-source CMake build (same target without precompiled headers)
workload: Qt Creator build on Windows 10 with target_precompile_headers (CMake merge request 3553 prototype) against the same build without precompiled headers, with three compilers.
claimed_speedup: Qt Creator: 22.09% speed-up with MinGW GCC 8.1.0, 37.28% with Visual C++ 2017, 30.66% with Clang-cl 8.0.0 (from search summaries of the Qt blog post; snippet only); the post says a few CMake lines give a 20-40% speed increase without changing sources.
compiler_and_flags: MinGW GCC 8.1.0, Visual C++ 2017, Clang-cl 8.0.0 (versions per search summary); flags and build type not shown
hardware: Windows 10 machine with an AMD Ryzen CPU (model not shown in the summary)
stars_or_usage: 8.1k stars (GitHub mirror of the upstream CMake repository); target_precompile_headers ships since CMake 3.16
tradeoffs: Implemented in Source/cmLocalGenerator.cxx (AddPchDependencies) with PRECOMPILE_HEADERS, INTERFACE_PRECOMPILE_HEADERS, SKIP_PRECOMPILE_HEADERS. Needs a sensible set of headers to precompile; a Qt mailing-list thread cited in search results argued that precompiling headers used only once or twice wastes time, and an ITK developer reported no significant reduction in their tests. Projects should avoid PUBLIC or INTERFACE precompile headers on exported targets (CMake docs).
caveats: Snippet only: www.qt.io could not be opened (host unresolvable from this container), so the percentages come from WebSearch result summaries of the 2019-08-01 Qt blog post and need re-checking on the page. Single machine, one project, 2019, measured on the pre-release merge request, not the shipped 3.16 code; CPU model and flags missing; the percentage definition (time saved or speed ratio) is not clear from the summary. The kitware/cmake repo carries the implementation and docs but no benchmark code or timings (Help/command/target_precompile_headers.rst has no numbers). The book's companion example (ch07/06-precompile, a hello-world) carries no timings.
